assertion.en: An echo sounder on a ship records a return after 4 s in seawater where sound travels at 1500 m/s, and this places the sea floor 3000 m below the ship.

reason.en: The recorded 4 s is the time for the sound to travel down to the sea floor and back up again, so the time spent travelling down is only half of it.

optionFeedback.b: Both statements are true, but the Reason does not account for the Assertion - it explains why 4 s has to be halved, not why the answer comes out at 3000 m. Work out the distance the sound covers in half of 4 s.
optionFeedback.c: The Reason is true, so it is not the false statement here. Halving the 4 s gives 2 s, and 1500 m/s × 2 s is 3000 m - the Assertion holds.
optionFeedback.d: The Assertion is not the false statement here - the sounder really does measure a round trip, and 1500 m/s × 2 s is exactly 3000 m.

explanation.en: Both statements are true, and the Reason does explain the Assertion. The sounder's clock stops when the echo comes back, so it times the whole journey: 4 s is 2 s down and 2 s back up. The depth is therefore 1500 m/s × 2 s = 3000 m. Using the full 4 s would give 6000 m, which is the distance there and back - double the depth. The same halving is needed in air, which is why an echo off a wall only gives you half the total distance the sound covered.

hints.en: Ask separately: is each statement true on its own, and only then whether the second one actually accounts for the first.
The sounder stops its clock when the echo arrives, not when the pulse leaves. So the 4 s has to cover both journeys - what is half of it, and how far does sound go in that time?
